nameStory: The lined anemone gets its common name from the distinctive lines or stripes that mark its body column. These linear patterns help distinguish it from other sea anemones in New England waters, making the name both descriptive and practical for identification.
description: The lined anemone is a marine animal that looks like an underwater flower but is actually a predatory creature related to jellyfish and corals. It has a cylindrical body column topped with a ring of stinging tentacles that surround its mouth. These anemones are typically small to medium-sized, living attached to hard surfaces in deeper coastal waters. Unlike the colorful anemones you might see in tide pools, lined anemones tend to have more subdued coloration with their characteristic striped pattern.

idTips.label: Linear striping pattern
idTips.description: Look for distinct lines or stripes running along the body column - these may be lighter or darker than the base color and give the anemone its name

idTips.label: Cylindrical body shape
idTips.description: The body column feels firm and smooth when gently touched, with a distinctly tube-like shape rather than bulbous or irregular

idTips.label: Ring of tentacles
idTips.description: Multiple tentacles surround the central mouth opening, feeling slightly sticky or clingy if you carefully brush against them

idTips.label: Attached base
idTips.description: The bottom end is firmly anchored to rocks, shells, or other hard surfaces and cannot be easily dislodged

idTips.label: Subtidal habitat
idTips.description: Found in deeper water rather than tide pools, typically requiring snorkeling or diving to observe clearly

habitat: Lined anemones live in the subtidal zone of New England's rocky coastlines, typically in water too deep to be exposed at low tide. They attach themselves to hard surfaces like rocks, shells, or pier pilings in areas with good water circulation. You'll most likely encounter them while snorkeling or diving in coastal waters rather than during shoreline exploration.

seasonality.spring: More active as water temperatures begin to rise, with tentacles fully extended for feeding during calm weather periods.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when warmer waters bring abundant plankton and small prey, making this the best time to observe their feeding behavior.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may begin to contract more frequently as water temperatures drop and storms become more common.
seasonality.winter: Often contracted into a tight column shape during rough weather, but still present and occasionally extending tentacles during calm periods.

funFact: Despite looking like plants swaying in the current, lined anemones are actually fierce predators that can catch and digest small fish - they're more closely related to jellyfish than to any plant, and their 'petals' are actually armed with thousands of microscopic harpoons!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other sea anemones, but the lined pattern on the body column is the key distinguishing feature. Remember: 'Lines on the body, lineata's the name' - other anemones may have colorful tentacles or different textures, but few show the characteristic striping pattern.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'Edwardsiella' honors French zoologist Henri Milne-Edwards, while 'lineata' simply means 'lined' in Latin. Don't confuse this marine anemone with Edwardsiella bacteria, which is a completely unrelated microorganism that causes disease in fish - they just happen to share similar names.
compareHints: Since this is the only Edwardsiella species commonly found in New England waters, compare it to other anemone families in the region. Unlike the colorful Northern red anemones or the large frilled anemones found in tide pools, lined anemones are distinguished by their subtidal habitat, smaller size, and most importantly, the linear striping pattern on their body column that gives them their name.
